characterList.description: A man wearing a salmon coloured polo shirt and glasses
characterList.name: Stephen Bosi

content_metadata.description: A video demonstrating and explaining the pinch effect, where parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other, and its application in lightning conductors.

qAndA.answer: It's a power supply capable of delivering a very large electrical current.
qAndA.question: What is the device on the left connected to the apparatus?

qAndA.answer: The apparatus has copper on the bottom and top with ten wires attached in parallel to them.
qAndA.question: What is the apparatus made of?

qAndA.answer: The wires pinch together when the power supply is turned on.
qAndA.question: What happens to the wires when the power supply is switched on?
What happens to the cables connecting the power supply and the apparatus?

qAndA.answer: It is a part of a lightning conductor that was crushed due to the pinch effect caused by a lightning strike.
qAndA.question: What is the copper pipe shown at the end?

scenes.contextualRelevance: The video demonstrates the practical application of electromagnetic forces in electrical engineering, particularly in lightning conductors.

narrativeProgression.description: Stephen Bosi introduces himself and the concept of the pinch effect.
The viewers are encouraged to pause the video and make predictions about what will happen when the power supply is turned on.
The power supply is turned on and the viewers see the effects on the wires and cables.
Viewers are prompted to pause and discuss their observations.
Stephen Bosi explains the observed pinch effect and its application in lightning conductors.
Stephen Bosi presents a crushed copper pipe from a lightning conductor.
Viewers are prompted to pause and discuss what might have happened to the copper pipe.

And they're connected in parallel so that when I turn on the power supply, I'm going

Now can any of you out there predict what's going to happen when I turn on the power supply?
Let's give it a whirl.

strange down here.

Now what I hope that you observed was that the wires became pinched together as the current
passed through them in the same direction.
So this reason that effect is sometimes called the pinch effect.
Now here's another interesting thing that might be related.
What I have here is a copper pipe that was found about a hundred years ago and it was
